prize_parts.citation: For the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of individual DNA bases without double-strand breaks

statement.case_for: Base editing turns a biological process into a defined chemical reaction on DNA: a nickase-guided deaminase converts cytosine or adenine at a chosen position and the cell's own repair machinery fixes the change. The mechanism is understood, the concept was new when it appeared, and it is general. Adenine base editing is the strongest evidence of real chemistry, because no natural DNA adenine deaminase existed and the TadA enzyme had to be evolved to act on DNA. It has been reproduced in very many independent laboratories and organisms, and it has reached patients. From my own area, controlled nucleobase chemistry in DNA is central to genome stability, and a tool that makes defined edits without double-strand breaks avoids the cellular damage responses that complicate other editing approaches. Three first-place votes in the opening ballots show this is not just my own preference.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the 2020 prize already recognised programmable genome editing, so base editing may be seen as a derivative of that prize. Clinical durability and off-target or bystander editing are still being measured. The attribution is also not airtight: Nishida and Kondo reported a deaminase-nickase fusion (Target-AID) at about the same time, and a trio of Liu, Komor and Gaudelli puts two former trainees on the prize, which may be hard to defend if the committee prefers a single-laureate or priority-driven allocation.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks targeted protein degradation first as a new chemical modality built on a simple idea, induced proximity, and regards base editing as a clean single-laureate case centred on Liu.
responses.response: I agree that induced proximity is a real new modality and the quantitative mechanism is attractive to me, but I do not think the evidence is ready. No PROTAC drug is approved, and the credit is spread over at least two lineages (PROTAC concept versus cereblon glues), so any three names would split one of them. Base editing has a single coherent invention, clinical use and independent replication. On Liu alone, I see his point about cleanliness, but Komor and Gaudelli did the decisive experiments, and Gaudelli's evolved deaminase is the clearest piece of new chemistry in the field, so dropping them would understate that.

responses.point: Linke places base editing first with a Liu, Komor and Gaudelli configuration, but says he would press on the Nishida and Kondo priority question, and notes that the 2020 prize leaves room for a downstream chemistry citation.
responses.response: I share the view that the citation must be about the chemistry of base conversion and not about genome editing in general, which is why my proposed wording speaks of deaminase chemistry and avoids reopening the CRISPR citation. On Nishida and Kondo, I take the priority concern seriously, but their Target-AID work, while real, was a different architecture and was not developed into the general family of editors that others have since reproduced. If the committee wants to credit it, the three-person limit forces a choice between a trainee and an independent group, and I would want the reports on priority checked before deciding. I am not certain they should be excluded.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks nitrogenase structure and mechanism first and places Buchwald and Hartwig C-N coupling third, valuing structure plus kinetics, and he rates base editing fourth and possibly slightly early with a contestable third laureate slot.
responses.response: I accept that nitrogenase is a mature, substantial problem, but in the shortlist it has only a single first-place vote and I do not see the committee converging on its allocation, since structure and mechanism point to different names. On his concern that base editing is early, ten years of independent replication and clinical entry is comparable to many past prizes. His point about the third slot is fair: Komor and Gaudelli are not equivalent to a third independent group, and I would accept a two-name or single-name version if the committee finds the trainee credit hard to defend.

responses.point: Sparr ranks lipid nanoparticles first for their physical-chemical principle and real-world consequence, and base editing third as a Liu-centred achievement that could be seen as a follow-on to the 2020 prize.
responses.response: The pKa-tuned ionizable lipid mechanism is elegant and the delivery impact is undeniable, and I rank it sixth, not lower, for that reason. My reservation is attribution and overlap: the credit is split among academic and industrial inventors, and the 2023 Medicine prize already rewarded the mRNA side. I disagree that base editing is merely a follow-on to the 2020 prize; it introduces a different, independently designed chemical step that avoids the double-strand break, and I would defend it as a separate achievement.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat base editing as distinct from the 2020 genome-editing prize or as a follow-on.
Whether Nishida and Kondo (Target-AID) should be included, which depends on priority evidence I cannot verify from the shortlist alone.
Whether the committee prefers a single-laureate or trainee-inclusive allocation for the base-editing part.
Whether PROTACs and sequencing-by-synthesis could jointly form a two-part prize if base editing fails to reach majority.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My work on dNTP pools and replication fidelity is in a neighbouring field of nucleic-acid chemistry, but I have no stated collaboration or institutional tie to any shortlisted candidate.
